subject: GRM/Sequential - Goodness of fit with missing values

messages.author: 051f9e22cdcba7f5
messages.subject: GRM/Sequential - Goodness of fit with missing values
parts:
Dear Dr. Chalmers,

I started to use the mirt package in order to evaluate difficulty estimations of programming tasks (about a hundred) I am providing to my students (more than a hundred). I have several questions that arise mainly from the fact I am an ordinary programmer and rather incidentally approach the deep waters of statistics. I hope you'll find time to help me understand some of the following subjects.

The data contains encoded number of attempts each student needed to solve a particular assignment. The number of allowed attempts equals 3, therefore matrix contains 3, if the student solved task on the first attempt, 2 - second attempt, 1 - third. 0 - failed to solve the task on any of the attempts. NA - if there was no attempt on the task by the user.

Example data:

ID01 ID02 ID03 ...
3    1    0    ...
NA   NA   0    ...
2    NA   NA   ...
...  ...  ...  

This is the format I use for the graded response model.

Q1. The first question is: what will be the valid format to encode data for the sequential response model?

The next problem I face is lots of NA's. There are very few students that attempted to solve all tasks. Most of them solved not more than about a half of tasks. I am unable to evaluate goodness of fit for this model with any of the methods provided in mirt package, as the data contains too much NA's. 

Q2. Is there any way of calculating goodness of fit in such situation?

Any help from you will be appreciated.

Thank you very much for the great piece of work you provide to the R community.

Best Regards
Maciek

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: GRM/Sequential - Goodness of fit with missing values
parts: Hi Maciek,

The data contains encoded number of attempts each student needed to solve a particular assignment. The number of allowed attempts equals 3, therefore matrix contains 3, if the student solved task on the first attempt, 2 - second attempt, 1 - third. 0 - failed to solve the task on any of the attempts. NA - if there was no attempt on the task by the user.

Example data:

ID01 ID02 ID03 ...
3    1    0    ...
NA   NA   0    ...
2    NA   NA   ...
...  ...  ...  

This is the format I use for the graded response model.

Q1. The first question is: what will be the valid format to encode data for the sequential response model?

The current format seems reasonable to me. The 'most able' students should be receiving a score of 3, while least able a 0. Though note that each participant should occupy a single row, not column (just use dat <- t(dat) to transpose the data).

The next problem I face is lots of NA's. There are very few students that attempted to solve all tasks. Most of them solved not more than about a half of tasks. I am unable to evaluate goodness of fit for this model with any of the methods provided in mirt package, as the data contains too much NA's.

The NA's aren't really a factor in IRT estimation, they just represent less information to use during estimation (at worse this increases the standard error estimates of the parameters). So long as the missing data mechanism is missing (completely) at random then you should be fine.
Q2. Is there any way of calculating goodness of fit in such situation?

Yes, the M2() function has a na.rm option to use in such situation, as does the itemfit() function for the fit of each respective item. Though given your test bank size you may only be able to use the latter unless you have a lot of time to wait and a good amount of RAM. HTH.

Phil

Any help from you will be appreciated.

Thank you very much for the great piece of work you provide to the R community.

Best Regards
Maciek

The current format seems reasonable to me. The 'most able' students should be receiving a score of 3, while least able a 0. Though note that each participant should occupy a single row, not column (just use dat <- t(dat) to transpose the data).

Sorry, I wasn't clear about the data format I presented. It's as it should be: participants -> rows, tasks -> columns. Correlation of the difficulty estimations from both models is 0.91. I asked the question as correlations I received previously were pretty low, however it was probably my mistake.

The next problem I face is lots of NA's. There are very few students that attempted to solve all tasks. Most of them solved not more than about a half of tasks. I am unable to evaluate goodness of fit for this model with any of the methods provided in mirt package, as the data contains too much NA's. 

The NA's aren't really a factor in IRT estimation, they just represent less information to use during estimation (at worse this increases the standard error estimates of the parameters). So long as the missing data mechanism is missing (completely) at random then you should be fine. 
 

Q2. Is there any way of calculating goodness of fit in such situation?

Yes, the M2() function has a na.rm option to use in such situation, as does the itemfit() function for the fit of each respective item. Though given your test bank size you may only be able to use the latter unless you have a lot of time to wait and a good amount of RAM. HTH.

I already previously ran the M2(na.rm = TRUE) function, however it confused me, as results I received were:

GRM: M2: 2122,825, df: 2622, p: 1, RMSEA: 0, RMSEA_5: 0, RMSEA_95: 0, SRMSR: 0,2606455, TLI: 2.516962, CFI: 1
Sequential: M2: 2093,157, df: 2622, p: 1, RMSEA: 0, RMSEA_5: 0, RMSEA_95: 0, SRMSR: 0,259721, TLI: 2.607798, CFI: 1

In my dataset there are about 300 rows (participants) and only 15 made attempts to solve all tasks. All other 284 rows contain NA's. Could you please clarify, how reliable are these results? Shouldn't I doubt when I see these sharp values of p = 1 and CFI = 1?

Maciek

Thank you very much for the great piece of work you provide to the R community.

Best Regards
Maciek

parts:
I already previously ran the M2(na.rm = TRUE) function, however it confused me, as results I received were:

GRM: M2: 2122,825, df: 2622, p: 1, RMSEA: 0, RMSEA_5: 0, RMSEA_95: 0, SRMSR: 0,2606455, TLI: 2.516962, CFI: 1
Sequential: M2: 2093,157, df: 2622, p: 1, RMSEA: 0, RMSEA_5: 0, RMSEA_95: 0, SRMSR: 0,259721, TLI: 2.607798, CFI: 1

In my dataset there are about 300 rows (participants) and only 15 made attempts to solve all tasks. All other 284 rows contain NA's. Could you please clarify, how reliable are these results? Shouldn't I doubt when I see these sharp values of p = 1 and CFI = 1?

You have good intuition, I too doubt the veracity of these results given only 15 full response vectors. At best these are tentative results that have not rejected the null of 'good fit', but given the data used this is probably very under powered. I don't think a theoretical solution for the M2 statistic with so much missing data has appeared in the literature yet, so at this point you may be stuck with only there conservative results.  

Phil

Maciek


Thank you very much for the great piece of work you provide to the R community.

Best Regards
Maciek

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: GRM/Sequential - Goodness of fit with missing values
parts:
The GRM model uses intercepts, not difficulty parameters (most of the package uses intercepts parameterizations actually, so the ordering will be reversed and the magnitudes slightly different than you would expect). Sequential and gpcmIRT are two notable exceptions where these only exist in the classical IRT discrimination-difficulty format. HTH. 

Phil
